Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
1044 AM EDT Sun Aug 2 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 215 AM EDT Sunday...

Isolated flash flood threat remains for late today into early 
Monday with the upcoming low pressure system due to potential 
for slow- moving showers and thunderstorms. Best potential for 
any localized flash flooding is across the northern Adirondacks 
and St. Lawrence Valley of New York.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 215 AM EDT Sunday...

1. Moderate to locally heavy rainfall through Monday with an
isolated risk of flash flooding.  

2. Seasonably warm and wet for the second half of next week and 
next weekend.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 215 AM EDT Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Interesting synoptic setup with vertically-stacked low 
pressure system centered across Indiana early this morning. A 
positive tilt mid-level trough extends newd from the closed low 
across sern Michigan into sern Ontario. This positive tilt trough 
should serve as a slow-moving focus for convergence and deformation, 
with ongoing showers and embedded convective activity likely to 
spread northeastward during the daylight hours today (Sunday). While 
best precipitation focus should be across the International Border 
into Ontario, may see some bands of moderate to locally heavy 
rainfall lifting across the St. Lawrence Valley later this morning 
into the afternoon hours. Combination of rich moisture (PW values 
1.9 to 2.0) and some training thunderstorm potential with SBCAPE 
values 500-1000 J/kg does bring potential for widespread 1-2" 
rainfall with locally higher amounts across St. Lawrence and 
Franklin Counties today. The 00Z HREF Probability Matched Mean QPF 
guidance suggest a few locations could see rainfall amts exceeding 
2" thru 12Z Monday. Topographically, it is relatively difficult to 
get flash flooding in the St. Lawrence Valley given flat terrain, 
and QPF values suggest only an isolated threat. Will continue to 
message this isolated threat via the Hazardous Weather Outlook. 
Narrow CAPE profiles with modest mid-level lapse rates suggest there 
isn't a severe threat with this activity. Have included heavy 
rainfall wording only into the forecast grids.  

Abundant clouds across the St. Lawrence Valley and the Adirondacks 
will keep high temperatures generally in the 74-78F range this 
afternoon. Rain generally holds off across Vermont thru early 
evening, and partial sunshine allows temperatures to reach the lower 
80s in most locations from the Champlain Valley ewd. 

For tonight and Monday, wave low moving newd across the Eastern 
Great Lakes and across the St. Lawrence Valley will eventually allow 
the baroclinic zone to shift ewd as as cold front tonight into 
Monday. It appears the bulk of the widespread shower and embedded 
thunderstorm activity will be 06-18Z Monday from the Champlain 
Valley ewd associated with strengthening low-level frontal 
convergence and right entrance region of impressive 90-100kt 250mb 
jet for this time of the year. Have indicated 80-100% PoPs overnight 
into Monday morning, gradually diminishing thereafter as best 
dynamic support and PWATs shift east of our forecast area. Overall 
rainfall amounts from the Champlain Valley ewd are expected to range 
from 0.5" to 1", with some locally heavier amounts possible due to 
thunderstorms. Flash flooding is not currently expected in VT. Highs 
on Monday will generally range from the upper 70s to lower 80s.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A typical mid to late summer set-up is in store for the 
second half of the upcoming week and next weekend. A strong Bermuda 
high pressure system (nearly 600 dm) is forecasted to situate across 
the western Atlantic with an elongated but not highly amplified 
trough across the northern US. This will keep the longwave pattern 
Thursday through Sunday relatively the same with several rounds of 
shortwave energy aiding the longwave trough from falling apart. The 
North Country will be in a peculiar spot between the ridge and main 
upper level trough which should help bring warmth, moisture, and the 
occasional shortwave trough overhead. Basically, this means that we 
should see periods of showers and possibly a few thunderstorms daily 
with temperatures hovering within a few degrees of normal (generally 
low to mid 80s). No significant storm systems appear likely on the 
horizon given we have no distinguishable surface features to produce 
convergence/lift and modest flow aloft. High PWAT values in the 90+ 
percent range will allow any showers or thunderstorms that develop 
to be heavy rainers but they will be scattered at best and short-
lived, meaning flooding isn't a concern at this time.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z SUNDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Through 12Z Monday...We've already begun to see a few showers
move through KMSS this morning but the latest radar trends show
a noticeable break for much of the morning. Widespread rainfall
is on track to move into northern New York this afternoon with
rain slowly pushing eastward through the evening. It will likely
take until 06Z before rain moves into the Vermont terminals
while northern New York should see rainfall between 18Z and 00Z.
MVFR to brief IFR conditions are possible within this rain given
a very moist environment and visibility reductions will likely
be tied to convective elements embedded within the showers.
Winds will be from the south at 10 to 20 knots ahead of the
rainfall with winds diminishing below 10 knots at the onset of
the rain showers. Wind shear is likely to develop as winds
weaken with winds at 2000 ft around 40 knots.

Outlook...

Monday: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA, Chance
TSRA.
Monday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight chance
SHRA.
Tuesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday: VFR. Chance SHRA.
Wednesday Night: VFR. Chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Thursday: VFR. Chance SHRA, Chance TSRA.

&&

.MARINE...
As of 1041 AM EDT Sunday...

A Lake Wind Advisory is in effect for the broad and northern
waters of Lake Champlain until 8 PM today. South winds ahead an
approaching frontal system will lead to increasing winds on 
Lake Champlain enhancing gusts and wave conditions. Winds and
gusts on the lake will increase to 15 to 25 knots through this
afternoon. Waves will be generally 1 to 3 ft. Gusts will weaken
back to around 10 to 15 knots after sunset this evening.

&&

.CLIMATE...
Possible heavy rainfall tomorrow into Monday could approach
daily rainfall record levels. Below are the current daily
precipitation total records that may be broken at our area
climate sites.
